themes.name: Complex feelings about AI's role in mental health support
themes.description: Participants express a nuanced view of AI chatbots as accessible and non-judgmental tools valuable for minor emotional support and academic stress, yet emphasize the irreplaceable value of human empathy, confidentiality, and specialized help for serious mental health issues.

resolved_code_refs.name: Preference for human support in emotional wellbeing over AI
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express a clear preference for human interaction over AI for emotional or wellbeing support, citing the importance of empathy, trust, and personalized care that AI chatbots cannot provide, especially for delicate or serious emotional issues.

resolved_quotes.text: I just do n't trust that with , like , my information and my personal life I do n't know , it 's a bit scary .
I don't think they can provide... like, the support that a human gives you, if that makes sense?
I just feel like, yeah, AI is smart and it's clever, but I just feel like it can't give you the same level as... a human.
At a certain point , it is better to talk to a person , because a person can help you .
There 's not really , like , an online resource that I would use . I would just , like , go to people around me .

I think it would just give you , like , generalized responses , so if you 're having , like , a really personal issue , I think it 's not gon na help you in the way it needs to , I guess , because it 's , like , automatic responses , right ?
I do n't think it 's , like , the solution to people 's well-being , just because I think , like , human interaction is really important to , like , get people to do better .
For something as sort of delicate as that, I think it needs more of a human touch ... I don’t think that it’s safe really, to use AI for that sort of thing.

resolved_code_refs.name: Need for human access alongside AI for emotional support and referrals
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants emphasize that AI chatbots for emotional support should be supplemented by accessible human professionals who can intervene, provide referrals, or offer deeper connection, viewing AI as a starting point rather than a full replacement for human contact.

resolved_quotes.text: there 'd need to be , like , a proper person at the end of , like… accessible still . At the end of it , you know , they would need to be able to , like , refer you , potentially , to someone .
Yeah , it 's a good… maybe as a little starting point .

resolved_code_refs.name: Importance of human support and concern about AI replacing services
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants emphasize that AI should supplement, not replace, existing human wellbeing services. Reassurance about AI as an 'add-on' that supports minor issues while maintaining real human help is important for user confidence and acceptance.

resolved_quotes.text: I think the important thing is to make sure that Students do n't know that… or students are confident that it 's not something which is replacing another service . Because that 's a , you know , that 's a big thing , is… AI replacing things .
I think the chatbot would be better as something alongside someone needing help , not the only source of help .

we 're thinking , obviously , you 've got the student wellbeing service that you can go to , and then this will just be as an add-on , and more for , like , the minor . situations . Um , just to get people started and sort of in a triage way kind of .

resolved_code_refs.name: Limited perceived benefit of AI chatbot for students with serious mental health issues
resolved_code_refs.description: This code reflects the perception that while AI chatbots may assist students with minor concerns, students with serious mental health issues may not find AI support as beneficial, implying a need for more specialized human support for serious conditions.

resolved_quotes.text: Students with more serious mental health issues .

resolved_code_refs.name: AI as an easier and more accessible mental health support option
resolved_code_refs.description: This code captures the perception that AI chatbots can significantly improve accessibility and ease of obtaining mental health support for students, breaking down barriers to initial help seeking and providing a supportive, approachable option for mental wellbeing.

resolved_quotes.text: I think it could make getting help for mental health stuff a lot easier and more accessible .

it means , yeah , more people can access help and it 'll be a lot easier way for . people to go further into student services if they need it , or if they just need someone to talk to , then they have that .

resolved_code_refs.name: Comfort and openness to using AI for anonymous emotional support
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express comfort and openness to using AI chatbots for emotional support, appreciating the anonymity, absence of social judgment, and the ease compared to human interaction for sharing emotions and seeking wellbeing support.

resolved_quotes.text: I do n't find as peculiar , because I understand it from the standpoint of there 's no other person that could be judging you on the other end . ... Easier .

resolved_code_refs.name: Chatbot preferred for non-judgmental and safe emotional space
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants favor chatbots over human interaction because chatbots provide a non-judgmental, safe, and private environment. This space fosters openness without fear of judgment or embarrassment and allows immediate, unbiased responses, promoting comfort especially during sensitive emotional conversations.

resolved_quotes.text: I feel like there would be no judgment coming from the other side . It 's just… It 's a safe space ... resolved_code_refs.name: Reluctance to use AI chatbots for personal emotional or wellbeing support
resolved_code_refs.description: Several participants indicate low likelihood of using AI chatbots for their own emotional or wellbeing support due to mistrust, discomfort, or uncertainty about their helpfulness, preferring traditional human support mechanisms.

resolved_quotes.text: Probably not likely .
I do n't know if I would . I 've never , like , tried to . I do n't know if it would be helpful .

resolved_code_refs.name: Skepticism and nervousness about using AI for emotional wellbeing support
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express doubts and nervousness about the effectiveness and safety of AI chatbots for emotional support, acknowledging the human availability challenges but remaining wary and wanting to test AI extensively before trust is given.

resolved_quotes.text: Um , I do n't think it 's the greatest idea , but I understand why people are n't always available or chatbot would be . I get that .
I think I feel a little bit nervous , really . I 'd have to test it out . I like to test things out before I fully commit . It 's a new area , I suppose , these chatbots .

resolved_code_refs.name: Conditional willingness to use AI chatbot based on personal need
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express willingness to use the AI chatbot for wellbeing support only if they experience mental health or personal problems, showing that engagement depends on perceived relevance and necessity rather than proactive or preventive use.

resolved_quotes.text: Yeah , I would , if I actually had a problem .

resolved_code_refs.name: Value of accessible, private chatbot support to overcome barriers and stigma
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants value AI chatbots for their accessibility anytime and private use, helping overcome stigma related to mental health. Chatbots are seen as convenient for those hesitant to seek traditional help due to practical or emotional barriers, including language and social isolation issues.

resolved_quotes.text: With people who are concerned about the stigma around mental health , I 'd say this is something I 'd use . because of something you can just , you know , [...] you 're in bed , no ones around , and you can just quickly go on it . No one need to know .

You have to speak to GPs who might not always , you know , understand what ... in my experience , they 're not taking me quite seriously all the time , so I feel like this would be quite big help to people in such situations .

For example, like exchange students who, obviously, there could be a language barrier there, and they don't feel like they could speak to anyone. I do think that's a good way, because I've heard some horror stories about exchange students not being able to talk to people.

Yeah, potentially students who've like learning disabilities. So maybe like autistic students. People that feel, like, a bit excluded, people that don't really have anyone to turn to, that haven't really clicked with anyone at uni.

themes.name: Privacy concerns and trust balancing safety and confidentiality
themes.description: Participants reveal tensions between valuing privacy and accepting monitoring features that flag risk and enable intervention. Hesitations about confidentiality, flagging consequences, and fear of burdening others constrain openness, while safety mechanisms are appreciated as safeguards aligning with traditional wellbeing practices.

resolved_code_refs.name: Concerns about AI privacy and intrusive data access
resolved_code_refs.description: This code captures participants' fears and discomfort regarding AI's access to personal data, emphasizing worries about privacy invasion, tracking through cookies and phones, and the omnipresence of AI across platforms. It highlights the need for control and caution in AI's widespread use.

resolved_quotes.text: Probably just , like , the fact that they can , like , kind of , like , see your data and stuff , and then that whole , like , cookies thing as well , where they can , like , see your phone and all that . resolved_code_refs.name: Strong value placed on privacy with conditional openness to monitoring for safety
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants strongly value privacy in chatbot conversations, preferring limited sharing except when risk to self is flagged. Acceptance of monitoring features depends on individual needs, with willingness to be contacted for serious concerns like self-harm.

resolved_quotes.text: I’m a very big advocate for privacy ... if you don’t want something to be shown to others, then you should not have that thing shown to others ... Unless there’s a specific thing that’s been plugged up ... Overall, I think keeping that sort of chat private is good.

resolved_code_refs.name: Value and trust in AI safety and monitoring features
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants appreciate and trust AI chatbots that have safety mechanisms such as risk flagging for serious or concerning messages. These features provide a safety net by ensuring timely human intervention while respecting user privacy, similar to traditional wellbeing service processes.

themes.name: Chatbot design and interaction shaping user comfort and engagement
themes.description: Participants value chatbots that resemble familiar messaging apps, use friendly and simple tones, and incorporate calming visuals and conversational style. Personalized, gentle, and spaced check-in nudges are preferred to maintain connection without causing irritation or pressure, enhancing approachability and sustained engagement.

resolved_code_refs.name: Chatbot design resembling familiar messaging apps for approachability
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants appreciate chatbot designs that mimic familiar messaging platforms like WhatsApp or texting friends and family. This similarity enhances approachability, comfort, and ease of use, making technology for wellbeing support feel more natural and user-friendly.

resolved_quotes.text: Um , I mean , it feels like you 're texting , like , your friends or family , so I 'd say yeah .
Yeah , I like how it 's just set up , like a messaging service .

Yeah . It 's good that it 's casual . If it were too… serious , it would probably put people off .

resolved_code_refs.name: Preference for friendly and simple chatbot tone
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants prefer chatbots to use a friendlier, less formal tone with simpler, shorter questions. This style makes interactions feel more natural and less intimidating, promoting a warmer, casual conversational experience in emotional support technology.

resolved_quotes.text: Maybe if it was something a little bit… More along the lines of… It was more friendly , maybe more , you know , like , instead of , like , longer sentences asking how you feel , maybe you could just say , how do you feel today ? resolved_code_refs.name: Positive reactions to calming chatbot design and style
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants respond positively to chatbot designs with calming visuals and a gentle, conversational style that reassures users and acknowledges feelings. This approach avoids interrogation or judgment, creating a feeling of safety and acceptance during interactions.

resolved_code_refs.name: Limited frequency and personalization of chatbot check-in nudges

They emphasize the value of personalization, allowing users to set or modify the frequency based on their emotional state, with preferences ranging from once a week to daily depending on need.

resolved_code_refs.name: Importance of limiting check-in nudges to prevent user irritation and pressure
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants highlight the importance of limiting chatbot check-in nudges to avoid user irritation, annoyance, or feeling pressured. They suggest setting maximum limits and enabling users to disable nudges to respect autonomy and maintain natural engagement.

resolved_quotes.text: I think it should have a limit to how many times it sends a message before it just… stops , because I feel like eventually it 's just going to be very apparent it 's just… Checking in on you . It could also come across as slightly . like , insulting to their , um…

resolved_code_refs.name: Preference for gentle and spaced check-in nudges to simulate conversational presence
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants prefer subtle and spaced follow-up nudges from the chatbot to gently check in without being intrusive. They suggest timed prompts that simulate a caring conversational presence and support, with intervals such as every 10 minutes, hourly, or every couple of days.

resolved_quotes.text: Maybe, like, 10 minutes is probably a good time to just be like, look, are you all right? And then maybe, like, another hour. And then maybe just, like, every day, if they still haven't, like, just daily, just to be like, are you alright? Like… kind of thing.

resolved_code_refs.name: Appreciation for frequent check-in messages that convey a sense of care and support
resolved_code_refs.description: One participant values receiving multiple daily check-in messages from the chatbot as it encourages continuous engagement and creates a feeling of being cared for, which is meaningful for emotional connection and support.

resolved_code_refs.name: Preference for chatbot to continue conversations after risk flagging
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express a preference for chatbots to not abruptly stop conversations after identifying risk. Instead, chatbots should continue gently, gathering context to avoid misunderstandings and keeping users engaged while awaiting human support. This approach recognizes the chatbot's limitations with language nuances like sarcasm.

themes.name: Diverse perceptions of AI usefulness and trust forming acceptance
themes.description: Participants show mixed openness to AI, influenced by familiarity, evidence of effectiveness, and privacy concerns. While curiosity and acceptance grow with demonstrated benefits, negative preconceptions and fears about AI’s authenticity, errors, and ecological impact temper enthusiasm and willingness to use chatbots.

resolved_code_refs.name: Mixed openness and skepticism about AI chatbot use based on familiarity and privacy concerns
resolved_code_refs.description: Participants vary in willingness to use AI chatbots, with familiarity increasing acceptance and skepticism prevalent due to novelty and privacy concerns. Awareness of risk flagging may reduce openness, while quality of chatbot design influences intent to use and recommend.

resolved_code_refs.description: Participants express concerns about AI lacking authenticity and honesty, giving overly positive or skewed responses rather than truthful feedback. resolved_code_refs.name: Negative preconceptions about AI as barrier to chatbot use
resolved_code_refs.description: This code captures participants' negative preconceptions about AI technology, which create caution or reluctance to use AI chatbots for mental health support. It highlights how prior experiences, mistrust, or anti-AI attitudes can act as barriers to engagement with AI-driven mental health tools.

themes.name: AI chatbot benefits for specific student groups and contexts
themes.description: Participants identify key groups such as introverted, isolated, first-year, international, and students with disabilities as likely to benefit from AI chatbots. AI is valued as an initial point of contact that reduces access barriers, especially during exam stress or minor emotional challenges, supporting vulnerable and isolated students.

resolved_code_refs.name: Chatbot as an introvert-friendly initial access point for support
resolved_code_refs.description: This code captures how chatbots are perceived as beneficial initial contact points for introverted or reluctant students. They help overcome barriers to seeking help by acting like digital receptionists that guide users into the support system.
